Gray, Lorie, Putzolu and Traiger (1975/76, Granularity of Locks in a Large Shared Data Base): granularity trades concurrency against overhead, with intention modes IS, IX and SIX and an ancestor rule; no figures (from a summary).
Kung and Robinson (1981, On Optimistic Methods for Concurrency Control): optimistic methods rely on backup and are meant for low-conflict uses (from a summary).

Agrawal, Carey and Livny (1987, Concurrency Control Performance Modeling): optimistic beats blocking with infinite or ample resources, and blocking beats optimistic with scarce resources or at medium to high utilization; the summaries give no figures (from a summary, blog.acolyer.org).
Agrawal, Carey and Livny (1987): blocking had the lowest response-time variance, and a 'fake restart' assumption inflated restart-based throughput in earlier work (from a summary; no figure).
Earlier studies of optimistic against blocking disagreed because of modelling choices.
note: The sentence follows the Agrawal sentence in the same paragraph and names no separate source; the file does not say how it is known.

claim: Berenson, Bernstein, Gray et al. (1995, A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels): snapshot isolation is not serializable, allows write skew, and uses first-committer-wins (from a summary).

Cahill, Roehm and Fekete (2008/2009, Serializable Isolation for Snapshot Databases): serializable SI keeps throughput 'approaching' SI in most cases, and SI is much faster than strict 2PL; no figure (from a summary).
Srinivasan and Carey (1991, Performance of B-tree concurrency control algorithms): the B-link algorithms gave the most concurrency and best performance in simulation; no figure (from a summary).

Johnson and Shasha (1990, A Framework for the Performance Analysis of Concurrent B-tree Algorithms) give an analytic model of response time and throughput for naive lock-coupling, optimistic descent and Lehman-Yao; no figure (from a summary, abstract missing).

Brun, Holmes, Ernst and Notkin (2011, Proactive Detection of Collaboration Conflicts): about 1 in 6 merges had a textual conflict, across nine projects and 3,562 merges (from a search snippet; the page gave no rates).
Brun et al. (same source): after merges, build failures in 3 of those projects were about 0.1%, 4% and 10% of merges, and test failures were 28% in one (from a summary, unconfirmed on the page).

A Characterization Study of Merge Conflicts in Java Projects (Virginia Tech; author not named in the file): across 208 Java repos, 15,886 scenarios had textual conflicts, 79 had build conflicts and 33 had test conflicts (from a summary).

Ghiotto, Murta, Barros and van der Hoek (2020, On the Nature of Merge Conflicts, 2,731 Java projects): 'up to 10-20% of merge attempts conflict' is a cited figure, not the study's own result (from a summary).
Vasilescu and Muylaert group (2016-17, merge conflicts and builds on Travis): in half the projects, 1 in 6 merge commits did not build (from a summary; the PDF was not readable).
Apel et al. (2011, FSE), structured and semistructured merge: fewer conflicts in 60% of merge scenarios, average 34%, across 24 projects (from a summary; the FSE2011 PDF was not readable).
ESEM 2015 replication: reduction in 55% of merge scenarios, average 62% in those (from a summary).

Cavalcanti, Borba and Accioly (2017, Evaluating and Improving Semistructured Merge): across 30,000+ merges in 50 projects, an improved tool halves reported conflicts and has at least 8% fewer false negatives (abstract as returned by the fetch tool).
note: The file's 'quoted' means the abstract text as the fetch tool returned it (lines 4-5); that tool returns a small model's summary.

claim: A 2019 study of semistructured versus structured merge finds the two differ in 24% of conflict scenarios (from a summary).
Structured and semistructured merge give fewer reported conflicts but more missed interference (false negatives), renaming raises conflicts, and the benefit is smaller for JavaScript.
note: The file gives no source for this sentence; the sourced rows are at lines 65-68.

claim: Javamex benchmark (quad-core i7, citing Java Concurrency in Practice pp. 242-3): a striped map gives almost n times the throughput of a single-lock map with n threads under contention (from a summary).
Sestoft lecture notes (ITU Copenhagen): striping helps up to 8 threads, and striping plus non-blocking reads held to 13 threads on a 32-core Opteron (from a summary).
Amdahl (1967): the speedup cap is 1/s, so a serial share s = 1% gives at most 100 (from a summary via secondary text).
Gunther's Universal Scalability Law (perfdynamics page): C(N) = N / (1 + a(N-1) + bN(N-1)); with b = 0 it reduces to Amdahl, and with b > 0 throughput peaks at N = sqrt((1-a)/b) (from a summary).
note: The peak formula is stated in the file's scheme at line 80; the table row at line 86 cites Gunther for the formula, peak N and the Amdahl case at b = 0.

claim: Gunther (2008, A General Theory of Computational Scalability Based on Rational Functions): the USL equals a machine-repairman queue throughput bound, and Amdahl and Gustafson are corollaries (abstract as returned by the fetch tool).
note: 'quoted' here means the abstract text as the fetch tool returned it (lines 4-5).

claim: Gustafson (1988, scaled speedup): serial fractions of 0.4-0.8% gave speedups on 1024 processors (from a summary).

claim: The same study (arXiv 2607.04697) reports only 0.5% of co-active agent PR pairs were cross-agent (from a summary).
The same study (arXiv 2607.04697) reports 84.4% of conflicted files were source code, and nearly 42% of conflicts were modify/delete or add/add (from a summary).
AgenticFlict (Ogenrwot and Businge, 2026, arXiv 2604.03551): of 142K agent PRs, 107K simulated, 27.67% had textual conflicts and there were 336K conflict regions (from a summary).
AgenticFlict (same source): conflicts were over 1.1% of rejections (from a summary).

CodeCRDT (2025, arXiv 2510.18893): in 600 trials, parallel agents were up to 21.1% faster on some tasks and up to 39.4% slower on others, with semantic conflicts at 5-10% and 100% convergence (from a summary).

Co-Coder (2026, cohesion-aware task partitioning, arXiv 2606.00953): on 28 tasks, up to 2.10x wall-clock speedup and up to 35% lower API cost, and pass rate rose 14.0 points (20.1% to 34.1%) on CodeProjectEval (from search snippets).
